clue.text: Design that's permanent and vulgar as well

parts.note: tat is cheap, tasteless stuff, so vulgar gives this short word
as well means also, in addition

explanation.surface: Someone sniffs that body art is both indelible and common.
explanation.definitionFit: Ink pricked into the skin makes a picture that cannot be washed off, a lasting design on the body.

clue.text: Silk gets brief, thanks to French cheese

parts.note: ta is a short, informal British way of saying thank you
feta is a crumbly Greek cheese

explanation.surface: A silk merchant swaps fabric for some continental cheese, with a curt word of gratitude.
explanation.definitionFit: A crisp, lustrous woven fabric traditionally made of silk, used for gowns and linings.

clue.text: Sweat it out about upper-class type with surprising result

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters sit around the next piece
out signals that the letters of the words before it are worked out into a new order

parts.note: a toff is British slang for a posh, upper-class person

explanation.surface: Someone sweats over a posh person and gets an unexpected outcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' makes TWISATE, the anagram of the first two words, and 'about' wraps it round the posh person. 'Sweat it out' reads as one idiom, but 'out' is the anagram signal; toff is British slang for an upper-class type.
explanation.definitionFit: An unexpected turn of events that fortune deals is an idiom for a surprising result.

clue.text: Solvers in demand after nothing like Cyclops

indicators.note: after places the following piece behind the nought

parts.note: nothing is zero, shaped like the letter O

indicators.note: in means the solvers go inside the word for demand

parts.note: to demand something is to need it
ye is the old plural 'you', addressing the solvers

explanation.surface: A demand for crossword solvers is likened to the mythical giant.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cyclops of Greek myth had a single eye in the middle of the forehead.

clue.text: Call back to London and put in confinement

indicators.note: back tells us the word for call is read in reverse

parts.note: to dial a number is to call someone
going up to London is the British idiom for travelling to the capital

explanation.surface: Someone phones back and is told to come to the capital, then gets locked away.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone confined to bed by illness or injury is said to be out of action in this way.

clue.text: Upper-class type gets into fight at sale

indicators.note: gets into means the first piece is placed inside the second

parts.note: action is combat or fighting
U is the letter (type) meaning upper-class, from the U and non-U distinction

explanation.surface: A posh person ends up in a brawl at a sale.
explanation.walkthrough: U as 'upper-class' comes from 1950s British usage, U versus non-U speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A public sale where goods go to the highest bidder.

clue.text: Complaints heard from some Indian social groupings

indicators.note: some tells us only part of the next word is used, a run of its letters

parts.note: tribes are social groupings of people

explanation.surface: People grumble about certain communities in India.
explanation.definitionFit: Bitter verbal attacks or tirades, the kind of complaint an audience hears out loud.

clue.text: Plain plastic setting for silver leaf constructed

indicators.note: setting for means the rearranged letters form a setting around the jewel-like silver
plastic means pliable and reshaped, so the letters of plain are moulded anew

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A plain plastic mount for a silver leaf is being made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plastic' makes PINAL (an anagram of PLAIN), and 'setting for' mounts it round the silver like a jewel setting. Read 'leaf constructed' as one hyphenated idea: made of leaves, or pages.
explanation.definitionFit: Paginal means relating to pages, so something built of leaves (pages) fits loosely.

clue.text: Bravo, Boatman! Going west in carriage for upper-class type?

parts.note: B is Bravo in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the setter, Boatman, refers to himself as I

indicators.note: in means the compass point goes inside the vehicle

parts.note: a gig is a light two-wheeled horse-drawn carriage

explanation.surface: Applause for the setter as he heads west in a carriage, perhaps as a toff.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves by name, giving I or ME.
explanation.definitionFit: An important, powerful person, loosely an upper-class figure, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Use force (if clumsily) before reaching corrupt leader

indicators.note: before puts the first jumble ahead of the second
clumsily means the words in brackets are handled badly and jumbled
corrupt means the letters of the next word are spoiled and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone advises applying force, if awkwardly, before getting at a crooked boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clumsily' turns FORCEIF into OFFICER; 'corrupt' turns REACHING into INCHARGE.
explanation.definitionFit: The person with authority over an operation or unit is its leader.

clue.text: See 18 down
Vibration heard from upper-class car in old liberal circles

indicators.note: circles means the old party surrounds the other pieces

parts.note: the Whigs were the forerunners of the Liberal Party
RR stands for Rolls-Royce, the archetypal posh car

explanation.surface: A buzzing noise comes from a Rolls amid an old political crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circles' puts the old party round RRIN. A Rolls-Royce is the stock British emblem of wealth, and the Whigs were the forerunners of the Liberal Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A continuous buzzing or humming sound made by something spinning or vibrating quickly.

clue.text: Guardian to be like Spectator, the bounder?

parts.note: a spectator watches, so being like one means to watch
a dog is an animal that bounds about, playfully a bounder

explanation.surface: A newspaper takes on a rival magazine's role, calling it a cad.
explanation.walkthrough: Guardian and Spectator look like publication names, but here they are ordinary words.
explanation.definitionFit: A body that monitors and protects standards is a guardian of them.

clue.text: Get from A to B around eg Hackney

indicators.note: around means the letters are moved about and rearranged

explanation.surface: Travelling between points, perhaps through a London district.
explanation.walkthrough: A and B are musical keys, not places; Hackney is an area of east London.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving music from one key such as A to another such as B is modulating.

clue.text: Upper-class type has totally wrong delivery

parts.note: nob is British slang for a wealthy, upper-class person
all means wholly, totally

explanation.surface: A posh person is utterly mistaken.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a delivery the umpire rules illegal is called by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: An illegal ball bowled in cricket, which gives the batting side a run.

clue.text: See 2
See 19
Try out coherently defined social grouping

indicators.note: out says the letters of the word try are taken away from the rest
defined is read as reshaped, so the remaining letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone attempts to define a class of society clearly.
explanation.walkthrough: Take TRY out of COHERENTLY, leaving CHEELON, and 'defined' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: A rank or level in a hierarchy or organisation, so a social tier.

clue.text: Upper-class address of cricketer's joint

parts.note: Lord's is the famous London cricket ground, the cricketer's home
the hip is a joint of the body

explanation.surface: A form of address is attached to a sportsman's aching hip.
explanation.walkthrough: LORD'S is the London cricket ground; 'His Lordship' is how a peer is addressed.
explanation.definitionFit: A title of respect used when speaking to or of a peer, a noble form of address.

clue.text: Upper-class type on seashore before pole attempt …

parts.note: the land's edge is where it meets the sea, the shore
N is the north pole
a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: A posh person on the beach prepares for a trip to the Pole.
explanation.walkthrough: The break falls as LAND EDGE + N + TRY, not LANDED + GENTRY.
explanation.definitionFit: Landowning families form a class of the British upper ranks.

clue.text: … his pole attempts were ultimately for insane fun when getting lost

annotationWithheld.clue: … his pole attempts were ultimately for insane fun when getting lost

clue.text: Admit it's fashionable: what Boatman reportedly did for this word

parts.note: in means fashionable, trendy

indicators.note: reportedly says the following word is heard rather than seen

parts.note: the setter wrote a clue for this word, so he clued it

explanation.surface: The setter concedes it is trendy and comments on his own work.
explanation.definitionFit: To admit someone or something is to let it in, to include it as part of a group.

clue.text: Grow subsequently, following nitrogen injection in limb

indicators.note: following means the next piece comes after the first
injection in means the element is injected inside the limb

parts.note: a leg is a limb
N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen
then means afterwards, subsequently

explanation.surface: A leg grows after a medical injection.
explanation.definitionFit: To grow longer is to extend, so the two verbs share a sense.

clue.text: Detect water or steam

definitions.meaning: to detect is to spot or observe something
water and steam are forms of H2O other than its frozen one

explanation.surface: Someone spots liquid or vapour.
explanation.definitionFit: To spot something is to perceive it; the second reading splits as NOT ICE.

clue.text: Extract and heat a black instrument

indicators.note: extract signals letters drawn out from within the following words

explanation.surface: Instructions to extract something and heat it in a dark pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extract' takes TABLA from heaT A BLAck; a tabla is a pair of small Indian drums.
explanation.definitionFit: A pair of small hand drums used in Indian classical music.

clue.text: Working-class and drunk? A libellous slur!

indicators.note: a slur is a drunken run of words, so the letters before it are slurred together into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone insulted as a working-class drunk protests at defamation.
explanation.definitionFit: Manual workers without training form much of the working class.

clue.text: Saw abstract of essay in Guardian

indicators.note: abstract of means a short extract drawn from the words that follow

explanation.surface: A proverb is quoted in a summary of a newspaper essay.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old proverb, a familiar maxim.

clue.text: Incomplete sentence for alleged disturbances

indicators.note: alleged signals the word is as said aloud, not as spelt

parts.note: frays are brawls or disturbances

explanation.surface: A judge hands down only part of a sentence for alleged riots.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of words that does not form a full sentence is a fragment of one.
